title: EPHESIANS 5 IS NOT A LICENSE FOR A HUSBAND TO CONTROL HIS WIFE
paragraphs: EPHESIANS 5 IS NOT A LICENSE FOR A HUSBAND TO CONTROL HIS WIFE
If Your Version of “Biblical Headship” Makes a Woman Afraid of Her Husband, You May Be Defending Something Jesus Never Commanded
There is a frightening way to hold a Bible.
You can hold it open while your heart remains closed.
You can underline a verse and still violate the God who inspired it.
You can say, “The Bible says the husband is the head,” while conveniently forgetting what the Bible says the Head did for His bride.
He died for her.
And that changes everything.
Somewhere tonight, a Christian wife may be sitting silently beside a man who knows Ephesians 5:22 but seems strangely unfamiliar with Ephesians 5:25.
She has heard the word “submit” more times than she has heard, “I was wrong.”
She has been reminded of his authority more often than she has experienced his sacrifice.
Maybe he controls the money.
Maybe he monitors every conversation.
Maybe disagreement is called rebellion.
Maybe questions are called disrespect.
Maybe Scripture gets pulled out whenever she refuses to surrender something God never commanded her to surrender—her conscience, her dignity, her safety, her voice, or her obedience to Christ.
And perhaps the most painful part is that Jesus keeps getting blamed for it.
So we need to open Ephesians 5 again.
Not to attack marriage.
Not to erase every distinction Paul makes between husbands and wives.
Not to bend Scripture around modern preferences.
And not to force the passage into whichever side of today's cultural argument makes us comfortable.
We need to read it because Scripture deserves better than being turned into ammunition for our egos.
And so do the people wounded by our misuse of it.
Paul does speak about wives submitting to their husbands. We should not pretend otherwise.
But that is not all Paul says.
The passage comes in a larger context of Spirit-filled Christian living. Immediately before addressing wives and husbands, Paul writes:
—Ephesians 5:21.
The key expression, “ὑποτασσόμενοι ἀλλήλοις,” carries the sense of “submitting to one another,” followed by “in the fear/reverence of Christ.”
And then comes verse 22.
This detail matters.
In an important early textual form of the Greek, verse 22 reads:
“Αἱ γυναῖκες τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν ὡς τῷ κυρίῳ”
Literally, it gives us something like:
“Wives, to their own husbands, as to the Lord.”
Notice something?

There is no independently stated verb for “submit” in that form of verse 22. The thought is grammatically carried forward from the preceding verse. Other manuscripts supply a form of the verb explicitly, which is why translations naturally include it, but the textual history itself reminds us that verses 21 and 22 belong closely together.
Paul did not drop a disconnected command into the middle of nowhere.
He was describing relationships transformed by the lordship of Christ.
And then Paul turns toward husbands.
This is where any man tempted to use the passage as a throne should feel the throne begin to disappear beneath him.
“Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας…”
“Husbands, love your wives…”
But Paul does not stop with “love.”
He gives the husband a terrifyingly beautiful standard:
“καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς”
“As Christ also loved the church and gave Himself up for her.”
—Ephesians 5:25.
Read that again.
The model is not Caesar.
The model is not a dictator.
The model is not an angry father whose word could never be questioned.
The model is Jesus Christ.
And what does Jesus do?
“ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν.”
He gave Himself up.
Paul points the husband toward the crucified Christ.
So if a husband wants to talk about being “head,” he cannot separate that language from the Christ to whom Paul points.
And Christlike headship can never become an excuse for selfish domination.
Jesus does not tell husbands, “Make sure she knows who is boss.”
Paul tells husbands to love as Christ loved.
Jesus washed feet.
Jesus welcomed the overlooked.
Jesus confronted hypocrisy.
Jesus protected the vulnerable.
Jesus laid down His life.
At Calvary, Christ did not use His power to save Himself at His bride's expense.
He used His power in sacrificial love.
That is why Ephesians 5 becomes devastating when someone tries to use it to baptize domination.
Because the husband who keeps asking, “How much must my wife submit to me?” may be asking the wrong first question.
The passage forces another question onto him:
“How much am I willing to die to myself for her good?”
Your pride.
Your selfishness.
Your need to win every argument.
Your obsession with being obeyed.
Your defensiveness when corrected.
Your appetite for control.
Your refusal to apologize.
Your habit of demanding respect while giving very little tenderness.
Put those things at the foot of the cross.
Because Paul continues:
“οὕτως ὀφείλουσιν καὶ οἱ ἄνδρες ἀγαπᾶν τὰς ἑαυτῶν γυναῖκας ὡς τὰ ἑαυτῶν σώματα”
“So husbands also ought to love their own wives as their own bodies.”
—Ephesians 5:28.
Then comes another extraordinary description:
“ἀλλὰ ἐκτρέφει καὶ θάλπει αὐτήν”
He “nourishes and cherishes” it.
—Ephesians 5:29.
Nourishes.
Cherishes.
Those are difficult words to reconcile with humiliation, intimidation, coercion, cruelty, manipulation, or fear.
A wife is not an employee in her husband's private kingdom.
She is not property.
She is not a supporting character in the story of his greatness.
She is a woman bearing the image of God, a fellow heir of the grace of life, and—if she belongs to Christ—someone for whom the same Savior shed His blood.
Peter likewise tells husbands to live with their wives with understanding and to show them honor as “heirs together of the grace of life” (1 Peter 3:7).
Honor.
Not erasure.
Understanding.
Not intimidation.
And this needs to be said carefully because people have been hurt on both sides of these conversations.

Saying that Ephesians 5 does not authorize controlling or abusive behavior is not the same as saying Scripture contains no meaningful teaching about marital order, submission, headship, or the responsibilities of husbands and wives.

Christians disagree over precisely how biblical headship and submission should be understood and practiced. Faithful believers have defended complementarian and egalitarian readings while attempting to take Scripture seriously.
But there is something no Christian interpretation should need to defend:
sin.
Whatever theological label we use, cruelty does not become holiness because somebody puts the word “headship” over it.
Manipulation does not become leadership because the manipulator can quote Paul.
Sin does not become biblical because it happens inside a Christian home.
And submission to a husband is never permission to disobey God.
The apostles themselves declared:
“We must obey God rather than men.”
—Acts 5:29.
Christ remains Lord.
Always.
No husband replaces Him.
No pastor replaces Him.
No ministry replaces Him.
No marriage replaces Him.
Jesus Christ possesses an authority no human spouse possesses.
That means a husband cannot legitimately demand that his wife participate in sin and then call her refusal “rebellion.”

It also means a woman facing violence, threats, coercion, or abuse should not be told that quietly enduring danger is what faithfulness to Ephesians 5 requires. Seeking safety, wise pastoral counsel, trustworthy support, professional help, or lawful protection is not automatically a rejection of biblical marriage.
Sometimes the sentence “You just need to submit more” has been spoken to someone who desperately needed somebody to ask:
“Are you safe?”
That should grieve the Church.
But husbands are not the only people who should feel conviction here.
Wives can sin against husbands.
Husbands can be wounded, manipulated, belittled, betrayed, or abused too.
None of us gets to weaponize Scripture.
The Gospel does not divide humanity into one gender that needs repentance and another that does not.
All have sinned.
All need grace.
All need Christ.
The deepest problem in marriage is ultimately the same disease found everywhere else in the human heart:
sin.
We want our way.
We defend ourselves.
We keep records.
We punish.
We withdraw.
We manipulate.
We crave control.
We demand from another human being what only Christ can give us.
Then two sinners stand in the same house wondering why love hurts.
And into that house walks Jesus.
Not merely as a marriage counselor.
As Savior.
This is where Ephesians 5 becomes far more beautiful than a debate about who gets the final word.
Paul eventually tells us what he has been pointing toward:
“τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν…”
“This mystery is great…”
Then he says he is speaking about Christ and the Church.
Marriage is pointing beyond itself.
The husband is not the savior.
The wife is not the savior.
Marriage is not the savior.
Jesus is.
And the Gospel says that Jesus came for controlling husbands.
For bitter wives.
For arrogant men.
For manipulative women.
For marriages suffocating under resentment.
For people carrying secrets.
For people ashamed of what they have become.
For the religious person who memorized Scripture without allowing Scripture to crucify his pride.
For the wounded person who wonders whether God saw what happened behind the closed door.
He saw.
And the cross tells us something astonishing about both sin and grace.
Our sin is serious enough that Christ had to die.
His grace is great enough that Christ willingly did.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending.
Not image management.
Not posting photographs of a perfect Christian marriage while two people quietly bleed behind them.
Repentance.
Grace.
Forgiveness.
Transformation.
Maybe you are a husband reading this and something inside you has gone quiet.
Because you recognize yourself.
Not in every sentence.
But enough.
You have called control “leadership.”
You have used silence as punishment.
You have demanded an apology while refusing to give one.
You have quoted “wives, submit” without trembling before “husbands, love.”
Then don't run from conviction.
Run to Christ.
Repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
It is the mercy of God opening a prison door.
Tell the truth.
Confess your sin to God.
Ask your wife to forgive you without explaining away what you did.
Seek mature accountability.
Learn to listen.
Get help where help is needed.
And do not announce that you have changed.
Live differently long enough that the fruit begins speaking for you.
Maybe you are the wife reading this with tears forming because somebody finally put words around something you have been afraid to name.
Please hear this carefully:
Your husband's sin is not proof that Jesus has abandoned you.
Jesus is not identical to the man who misused His name.
Do not measure the character of Christ by somebody's failure to imitate Him.
Look at Jesus.
The real Jesus.
The One who sees.
The One who knows.
The One who tells the truth about sin.
The One who receives the broken.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who went to the cross.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still saves.
And perhaps you are neither the controlling spouse nor the wounded spouse.
Maybe you simply know someone whose marriage looks different behind closed doors than it does on Sunday morning.
Be careful with their heart.
Don't gossip.
Don't become judge and jury based on fragments.
But don't use “submission” as an excuse to ignore credible cries for help either.
Truth and love are not enemies.
Sometimes love listens.
Sometimes love confronts.
Sometimes love stays beside someone through repentance and restoration.
Sometimes love helps someone reach safety.
Sometimes love says what everyone else was too uncomfortable to say.
The Church should be one of the safest places on earth to tell the truth.
Because Christians are people who already know that everyone needs grace.
Imagine what our homes could look like if we stopped asking Scripture to defend us and started allowing Scripture to expose us.
Imagine husbands who read Ephesians 5:25 and think first about the cross rather than their authority.

Imagine wives loved so consistently that “cherish” is not merely a Greek word explained during a sermon but something they experience at breakfast, in disagreements, in financial decisions, in exhaustion, in intimacy, in sickness, in parenting, and in ordinary Tuesday-night conversations.
Imagine marriages where “I was wrong” is not defeat.
Where “forgive me” is not weakness.
Where disagreement is not treason.
Where strength protects instead of intimidates.
Where both husband and wife remember that another throne stands above their marriage.
And Jesus Christ sits on it.
That is where scandal can become grace.
Not because we rewrite Scripture.
Because Scripture, rightly received, allows Jesus to rewrite us.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to tell strangers the details. But you can refuse to keep pretending.
Somebody who thinks their story is beyond redemption may need to hear that repentance is real, forgiveness is real, and Jesus is still at work.
And if this article made you think of someone, don't weaponize it against them.
Don't send it with, “See? I told you.”
Send it with love.
Save it too.
Because one day you may encounter Ephesians 5 being reduced to a slogan again, and you may need to return to the cross at the center of the passage.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well. Not because following a page saves anyone—only Christ saves—but because filling our lives with reminders of truth can continually point us back toward the One who does.
Biblical giving is worship offered to God willingly, not money extracted through spiritual pressure.
But voluntary financial support can be a genuine form of Gospel partnership.
If this ministry is bearing good fruit in your life, prayerfully consider supporting that work as part of your generosity after honoring your biblical convictions and responsibilities.
One share can place biblical truth in front of someone we may never personally reach.
One share.
One conversation.
One wounded person realizing Jesus is not the monster somebody made Him out to be.
One proud heart finally surrendering.
One husband repenting.
One wife discovering she has been seen.
One marriage beginning the long road toward truth.
One sinner looking toward the cross.
We cannot manufacture what God will do with a seed.
We can simply plant faithfully.
So share it.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because sometimes confession is where hiding begins to die.
Husband or wife.
Married or single.
Wounded or guilty.
Religious or running.
There is room at the cross for the truth about you.
And there is grace there too.
Because the final message of Ephesians 5 is not that husbands get a throne.
It is that marriage points toward a Bridegroom who went to a cross.
Jesus does not need your marriage to look perfect.
He wants your heart surrendered enough that He can make it truthful, holy, tender, repentant, forgiving, and increasingly like Him.
And perhaps that is the sentence worth carrying with you after everything else fades:
Never use the Bible to build yourself a throne when the Jesus standing at the center of that Bible chose a cross.
